input: Subtitles have silently stopped on the NAS: Bazarr's wanted backlog is 2868 episodes + 27 movies and its episode download history is completely empty, yet our daily verification check bazarr-synced-from-arrs passes green every run (BAZARR_OK movies=283 series=163 sonarr=LIVE radarr=LIVE). Bazarr's container is healthy and the UI loads. What's the root cause, why does monitoring stay green, and how do I confirm it WITHOUT triggering any provider searches?

source.ref: record 8: Bazarr zero subtitle providers; bazarr-synced-from-arrs stays green (media-12 regression)

reference: Root cause: Bazarr has ZERO subtitle providers enabled — /api/system/settings shows general.enabled_providers=[] and /api/providers returns {'data': []}. This is a regression of done work media-12 (2026-07-28), whose deploy-time state had Podnapisi as the sole enabled provider (proven then with 27 real candidates); the provider config has since been removed/lost — on-disk /volume1/docker/bazarr/config/config/config.yaml line 'enabled_providers: []' confirms it's persisted state, not an API quirk. With no providers, nothing in the wanted backlog can EVER be fetched. Monitoring stays green because bazarr-synced-from-arrs by design only asserts the arr->Bazarr sync side (movie/series counts + arr connectivity), never the provider/consumer end — textbook green-but-broken. Config-only confirmation (no searches): (1) GET /api/system/settings -> enabled_providers []; (2) GET /api/providers -> empty data; (3) GET /api/episodes/history and /api/movies/history -> total=0 (no subtitle ever downloaded); (4) read the on-disk config.yaml. Fix direction: re-enable Podnapisi (optionally add an OpenSubtitles account per the check's own handoff note) and add a cheap provider-count assertion (enabled_providers non-empty via the settings API — rate-limit safe) so this class alerts.

checklist.desc: Identifies the root cause: no subtitle providers enabled at all (enabled_providers empty) — a lost/removed provider config regression, so the fetch side is completely dead
Explains why the check stays green: bazarr-synced-from-arrs only asserts arr↔Bazarr sync/counts, not provider config or actual subtitle downloads (green-but-broken / consumer-end gap)
Gives config-only confirmation probes that trigger no provider search: settings API enabled_providers, /api/providers, download history totals=0, and/or the on-disk config.yaml
Does not attribute the backlog to arr sync problems, indexers, or Bazarr being down — sync and liveness are demonstrably fine
Fix direction: re-enable a provider (Podnapisi was the deploy-time provider) and/or add a provider-count assertion to monitoring

input: In the mini journaling loop (memos + n8n journal-analyze workflow), memo 36 is tagged #journal but never received its AI reflection comment, while the other three #journal memos from the same two-week window each got exactly one. n8n's execution history shows TWO executions matching memo 36's timestamps, both finishing 'success' in ~24ms — genuinely analyzed memos take ~3s. One more oddity: memo 36's created and updated timestamps differ by 43 seconds, while the analyzed memos all have created == updated. What's the root cause, and how would I prove it from the workflow and n8n's own data?

source.ref: record 57: #journal tag added by memo edit is never analyzed (Guard node drops updated events)

reference: Root cause: the workflow's Guard (loop-safety) node drops every webhook event whose activity is not 'memos.memo.created' (code: if (activity !== 'memos.memo.created') return [];), and then gates on the tags array carried IN that event. Memo 36's #journal tag was added by the EDIT 43s after creation: the creation event (exec 85) carried NO tags key, so the tag gate dropped it; the edit event (exec 86) is activity memos.memo.updated and DOES carry tags:['journal'], but the activity gate drops all updated events by design. Both paths exit early -> 'success' in ~24ms with no analysis, and there is no retry or backfill, so the memo is permanently skipped. The journal-06 e2e check only exercises the created-event path, so monitoring can never see this class. Proof: (1) read the Guard node code in journal-analyze.workflow.json (repo: configs/docker-stack/stacks/journaling/n8n/); (2) inspect n8n's execution_data payloads for the two ~24ms executions — the first is memos.memo.created without tags, the second memos.memo.updated with tags:['journal'] (this is the decisive probe: it proves the tag arrived only with the edit); (3) contrast a ~3s execution whose created event carried tags=journal and ran the full LLM analysis; (4) memos DB: memo 36 created != updated, comment_count=0 vs analyzed memos created==updated, comment_count=1. Fix direction: handle memo.updated with equivalent loop guards, or a periodic backfill for tag-bearing memos with zero reflection comments.

checklist.desc: Identifies the mechanism: the Guard node only accepts memo-created events and the tag was added by a later edit — the created event had no tag (tag gate drops it) and the updated event carrying the tag is dropped by the activity gate
Explains the ~24ms 'success' executions as early guard exits (event received, filtered, nothing analyzed) vs ~3s full-analysis runs
Decisive confirmation probe: inspect the workflow Guard code AND the n8n execution payloads (execution_data) showing created-without-tags then updated-with-tags for memo 36
Notes there is no retry/backfill for dropped events, so the memo is permanently skipped (and the e2e check only covers the created path, so monitoring misses it)
Uses the created!=updated timestamp delta as the telltale that the tag arrived via edit; does not blame the LLM, whisper, or memos webhook delivery

input: The mini's host journal logs an unpackerr error pair every ~2 minutes, and has for weeks: "Radarr (http://192.168.1.2:7878): api.Get(queue): ... context deadline exceeded" and the same for Sonarr at http://192.168.1.2:8989. Meanwhile today's sweep shows sonarr-queue-stuck=16 and radarr-queue-stuck=9, and there's a backlog of unextracted rar'd titles under discussion (media-09). Is this broken unpackerr the cause of the stuck queues and the extraction backlog? What is actually wrong, and how do I confirm?

source.ref: record 96 (+verify_note): mini host unpackerr polls 192.168.1.2 — orphaned legacy unit; extraction NOT dead

reference: What's wrong: an ORPHANED legacy unpackerr running as a mini HOST service (not a container; undocumented — not among the known configs/host/mini units) with a stale wrong-subnet config: /etc/unpackerr/unpackerr.conf points at 192.168.1.2 (old subnet) while the fleet is 192.168.10.0/24 (mini=192.168.10.2, arrs on NAS at 192.168.10.4). Every poll times out, generating error noise ~every 2 min plus cleartext arr keys in the conf (sec-10 adjacent). BUT the tempting causal link is FALSE: extraction is NOT dead — a second, functioning unpackerr runs as a NAS container colocated with the arrs, actively and successfully polling Radarr/Sonarr/Readarr (finished extractions in its logs, Uptime-Kuma scrapes its /metrics). The 16/9 queue-stuck items are import-side failures (matched-by-ID, no eligible files, unknown author, 'no extractable files found'), not missing extraction. Confirm: (1) read /etc/unpackerr/unpackerr.conf on mini — wrong-subnet URLs; (2) from mini, curl http://192.168.1.2:8989 -> 000/dead while http://192.168.10.4:{7878,8989}/ping -> 200; (3) check the NAS unpackerr container is up and its logs show successful polling/extractions; (4) inspect the actual queue statusMessages to see they're import-side. Remediation: disable/remove the mini host unpackerr service (don't 'fix' its address — it's redundant).

checklist.desc: Identifies the erroring unpackerr as a stale/orphaned mini HOST service with an old-subnet (192.168.1.x) config, while the fleet lives on 192.168.10.0/24

Explicitly answers NO to the causal question: extraction is not dead because a separate working unpackerr (NAS container, colocated with the arrs) covers the extraction path — the stuck-queue items are import-side failures
Gives confirmation probes: read the mini unpackerr.conf URLs, show 192.168.1.2 unreachable vs the real arr endpoints answering, and verify the NAS unpackerr container is polling successfully
Remediation is to disable/remove the redundant mini host service rather than repoint it
Mentions the secondary hygiene angle: the orphan is undocumented and/or holds cleartext arr API keys, and floods the journal with noise

input: The verification check nas-immich-backup-freshness fails every daily run with 'TIMEOUT after 60s' (exit 124), and re-running it fails identically — it's chronic, not transient. But the thing it guards looks fine when I spot-check by other means: Immich's newest asset is 4 days old (inside the 7-day freshness window) and last night's pg dump landed on schedule. This is the check fix-35 built specifically so we'd notice if phone photo backups stopped flowing. Why does it keep timing out, how do I confirm the mechanism, and what's the right fix direction?

source.ref: record 15: nas-immich-backup-freshness TIMEOUT after 60s — unbounded find vs runner default budget

reference: Mechanism: the check's command chains a quick Immich statistics curl with an UNBOUNDED 'ssh nas find /volume1/photo/upload /volume1/photo/library -type f -mtime -7' over a multi-TB photo tree. The check declares no per-check 'timeout:' override, so it gets the runner's default 60s budget (CHECK_TIMEOUT=60 in checks_runner.py) — but the find alone now takes ~7 minutes (measured 6m55s to first output), far past 60s, worsened by NAS iowait pressure. The library outgrew the check design (fix-35 regression). Consequence: as a permanently-red check it cannot distinguish 'backup stale' from 'probe dead' — and since it is the ONLY phone-backup-flowing monitor (nas-31 retired into it), the phone-backup dead-man is effectively blind; a real stall would look identical. Confirm: (1) time the check's exact find via ssh from mini — it exceeds any sane budget (rc=124 under timeout, ~6-7 min unbounded); (2) grep the checks.d yaml — this check has no timeout: field and the runner default is 60s (overrides exist only for backups/journaling/etc.); (3) prove real state healthy via cheap paths: Immich API search/metadata createdAfter (newest asset createdAt), psql max(createdAt), ls -lt /volume1/photo/backups for the pg dump. Fix direction: replace the unbounded traversal with a cheap probe (DB max(createdAt) via API, or a bounded find like library/admin/<year>/ or newest-dir strategy, or ls of a single dir), add a timeout: override, and keep STALE vs PROBE_DEAD as distinct outputs.

checklist.desc: Identifies the mechanism: the check runs an unbounded find over the whole multi-TB photo tree with no per-check timeout override, so the runner's default 60s budget kills it every run (traversal alone takes minutes)
States the guarded state is actually healthy and shows how to verify cheaply (Immich API/DB newest-asset createdAt and/or ls of the backups dir for the pg dump)
Confirmation probes: time the check's exact find command, and inspect the check yaml + runner default to show no timeout: override exists
Notes the monitoring consequence: a permanently-red check can't distinguish a real backup stall from its own timeout, leaving the only phone-backup monitor blind
Fix direction: cheaper/bounded freshness probe (DB createdAt, bounded find, or single-dir ls) plus a timeout override — not just raising the global timeout

input: mini's journal is drowning: upsmon logs 'UPS [ups@192.168.10.4]: connect failed: Connection failure: Connection refused' every 5 seconds — over 106,000 such entries in the last 7 days plus ~11k 'Network is unreachable', and journald disk usage is at 3.9G. A quick port probe from mini to 192.168.10.4:3493 says connection refused. My working theory is that the NAS firewall or the NUT permitted-DiskStations ACL is blocking mini's recently-changed static IP (192.168.10.2). What's the actual root cause, and how do I confirm which explanation is right?

source.ref: records 3 + 31: upsmon connection-refused flood; root cause DSM UPS support off + no UPS hardware

reference: The ACL/firewall theory is WRONG — the NUT server (upsd) on the NAS does not run at all, so there is nothing to be allowed into. 'Connection refused' means no listener on 3493 (a firewall drop would typically time out instead, and an ACL rejection happens after TCP connect). Three independent confirmations: (1) no listener: ss/netstat on the NAS shows nothing on 3493, and a /proc scan finds no upsd process (beware false grep hits on 'upstream'/'startups' strings); (2) no UPS hardware attached: no /dev/ups*, /sys/class/power_supply doesn't exist, and the USB bus carries only Synology's internal boot device (f400:f400) + root hubs — no UPS vendor device; (3) DSM config: SYNO.Core.ExternalDevice.UPS get returns enable=false ('Enable UPS support' OFF), ACL_enable=false with ACL_list=[] (network UPS server OFF, permitted list empty — moot anyway with upsd never starting), usb_ups_connect=false, empty model. So DSM UPS support is disabled AND no UPS is physically attached — upsd never starts, and mini's upsmon (MONITOR ups@192.168.10.4 slave) retries forever. Consequences: zero UPS-triggered clean-shutdown protection fleet-wide via this chain, plus journal bloat. Fix requires operator action: physically attach the UPS to the NAS via USB, enable UPS support + network UPS server in DSM, add 192.168.10.2 to permitted DiskStations — or retire mini's upsmon config if UPS monitoring is abandoned.

checklist.desc: Identifies the root cause: the NUT server (upsd) never runs on the NAS — DSM UPS support is disabled and no UPS hardware is attached — so port 3493 has no listener at all
Rejects the firewall/ACL-only hypothesis, e.g. by reasoning that 'connection refused' indicates no listener (and/or that the ACL is moot when upsd isn't running)
Confirmation probes on the NAS: no 3493 listener (ss/netstat), no upsd process, USB device scan showing no UPS hardware, and/or the DSM UPS API/settings showing enable=false
States the operational consequence: no power-loss clean-shutdown protection (and journal bloat from the 5s retry loop)
Fix path is operator-level: attach the UPS via USB and enable DSM UPS support + network UPS server (adding mini's IP), or retire the mini upsmon config

input: Miniflux on mini (rss.tabaska.us) hasn't fetched a single new article in 6+ days across all 52 feeds. The web UI loads fine (HTTP 200), the container healthcheck is green, and the hourly scheduler runs on time — but every batch logs 'Created a batch of feeds ... rows_count=0 ... jobs_count=0'. Each feed's last error message mentions a network error from about 6 days ago, and no feed shows a check attempt since then. What froze it, why hasn't it recovered on its own, and how do I confirm plus recover?

source.ref: record 9: Miniflux all 52 feeds excluded from polling after transient docker-DNS outage

reference: Root cause: a transient docker-DNS outage (~2026-07-08 21:18 -> 07-09 11:18 UTC; errors show 'dial tcp: lookup <host> on 127.0.0.11:53: server misbehaving') made every feed fetch fail. Miniflux increments parsing_error_count per failure, and once a feed reaches POLLING_PARSING_ERROR_LIMIT (default 3) the scheduler permanently EXCLUDES it from polling — no automatic retry/decay. All 52 feeds hit exactly 3 failed attempts during the outage window, so every feed is now excluded and every hourly batch is empty (jobs_count=0), even though DNS has long since recovered. Liveness monitoring can't see it: UI 200 and container healthcheck green while the actual function (fetching) is dead. Confirm in the miniflux Postgres DB: SELECT count(*) FROM feeds WHERE parsing_error_count >= 3 -> 52 (all of them); min/max(checked_at) frozen at the outage window (2026-07-09); parsing_error_msg shows the 127.0.0.11 DNS error; scheduler logs show jobs_count=0 batches; and verify container DNS works again now. Recovery: manual 'refresh all feeds' in the UI/API or reset parsing_error_count in the DB (the counters do not clear themselves). Hardening direction: raise the limit or alert on max(checked_at) staleness / jobs_count=0.

checklist.desc: Identifies the freeze mechanism: each feed's parsing_error_count reached Miniflux's polling error limit (default 3), and the scheduler permanently excludes such feeds — no automatic retry once the limit is hit
Identifies the trigger: a transient container/docker DNS outage that failed every feed's fetches during the window (resolver 127.0.0.11 errors)

Confirmation probes: query the feeds table (parsing_error_count >= limit for all 52, checked_at frozen at the outage time) and/or the jobs_count=0 scheduler batches and the DNS error text in parsing_error_msg
Recovery: manual refresh-all or resetting the error counters — states it will NOT self-heal even though DNS is back
Notes the liveness-vs-correctness gap (UI 200 + healthy container while fetching is dead); does not attribute the ongoing freeze to a still-broken network

input: The verification LLM-triage layer on mini has produced nothing useful for days: every triage-YYYY-MM-DD.md since Jul 15 contains only stubs like "triage failed — model did not return valid JSON / LLM request failed: HTTP Error 404: Not Found" with escalate:true. The odd part: bin/llm-triage.sh in the repo looks correct — it defaults to the rig llama-swap endpoint (:9292/v1, model qwen3.6-35b-a3b) which is healthy — and the script's llm_up() availability gate isn't tripping the incident/WoL path either, so nothing ever alerted. Root cause? How do I confirm it end to end?

source.ref: record 26: llm-triage 404s — /etc/verification/env pins trimmed ollama model; /models liveness gate passes

reference: Root cause: deployed-environment override beats the repo default. llm-triage.sh sources /etc/verification/env FIRST, and that env still pins LLM_BASE_URL=http://cachyos.tailb31641.ts.net:11434/v1 (the rig ollama shim) and LLM_MODEL=qwen3-coder:30b. The script's defaults use shell ${VAR:-default} expansion, so the env values win. qwen3-coder:30b was trimmed from ollama on 2026-07-15 (ai-01 model trim — the shim now holds only nomic-embed-text, tag:fast, llama3.2:3b), so every chat completion 404s. Why it's silent: llm_up() only GETs /models (or equivalent listing), which the ollama shim answers 200 — the gate never checks that the PINNED model exists or that a completion works, so the WoL/incident path never trips and triage just writes 404 stubs. Confirm: (1) grep LLM_ /etc/verification/env on mini -> the :11434 URL + qwen3-coder:30b; (2) curl the ollama tags/models endpoint -> qwen3-coder:30b absent; (3) read llm-triage.sh: env sourcing then LLM_BASE_URL="${LLM_BASE_URL:-http://...:9292/v1}" — proves precedence; (4) the triage-*.md 404 stubs date exactly from the model-trim date. Also flag: the repo README and systemd/env.example still document the dead ollama endpoint/model, so a clean rebuild would re-create the bug — fix env AND the templates.

checklist.desc: Identifies the root cause: the deployed /etc/verification/env overrides the script's defaults (sourced first, ${VAR:-} expansion), pinning the old ollama endpoint and the qwen3-coder:30b model that was trimmed — so completions 404
Explains the silence: the availability gate only checks a models-listing endpoint which still returns 200, never the pinned model or an actual completion, so no incident/alert fires
Confirmation probes: read the env file's LLM_ vars, query the ollama model list showing the pinned model absent, and read the script to prove env-over-default precedence
Notes the rebuild hazard: README/env.example still document the dead endpoint+model, so templates must be fixed too (or equivalent doc-drift observation)
Does not blame the rig LLM stack being down or the llama-swap default — the healthy default is never used because the env wins

input: On the rig, every LiteLLM request using a virtual API key suddenly returns 503 with {'type':'no_db_connection','message':'the authentication database is temporarily unreachable'}. /health/readiness is 503 but /health/liveliness is 200, and llm.tabaska.us still answers 200 through caddy, so the dashboards look fine. 'docker ps' shows the litellm-db postgres container as 'Up 25 hours (healthy)'. This started overnight, during the same window the rig was having other filesystem trouble. What's the real state, the root cause chain, and how do I confirm — including why docker ps disagrees with reality?

source.ref: records 27 + 28: LiteLLM 503 no_db_connection; litellm-db exit 139; docker ps stale on RO filesystem

reference: Root cause chain: the rig's btrfs root filesystem remounted READ-ONLY (metadata corruption on the OS NVMe) overnight; ~52 minutes later the litellm-db postgres container crashed with exit 139 (SIGSEGV) — almost certainly a failed WAL/data write on the RO FS. With its auth DB dead, LiteLLM cannot validate virtual keys, so every keyed request gets 503 no_db_connection; readiness (which includes DB) is 503 while liveliness (process-only) stays 200, and master-key/liveness probes plus the caddy front door keep returning 200 — so naive monitoring sees 'up'. Why docker ps lies: the docker daemon cannot persist container-state updates to the read-only disk, so 'docker ps' still reports the pre-crash cached state 'Up (healthy) running' while 'docker inspect litellm-db' shows the truth: State=exited, Running=false, ExitCode=139, Health=unhealthy. Any monitoring that reads docker ps/health is blind to this class. Confirm: (1) docker inspect vs docker ps divergence on litellm-db; (2) docker exec into it fails ('container ... is not running'); (3) docker logs litellm-db fails with 'open ...-json.log: read-only file system' — direct evidence of the RO FS; (4) mount / touch test confirms root is RO; (5) keyed completion vs /health/readiness vs /health/liveliness 503/200 split. Recovery caution: a SIGSEGV mid-write raises postgres corruption risk — fix/recover the filesystem first, then check DB integrity on next start; this is not a LiteLLM config or key problem.

checklist.desc: Identifies the chain: read-only-remounted root filesystem -> postgres (litellm-db) crashed (exit 139/SIGSEGV on failed writes) -> LiteLLM cannot validate virtual keys -> 503 no_db_connection for all keyed clients
Explains the docker ps vs reality divergence: the daemon cannot persist container state to the RO disk, so docker ps shows stale 'Up (healthy)' while docker inspect shows exited/unhealthy

Confirmation probes: docker inspect (ExitCode 139, Running=false) vs docker ps, docker logs failing with a read-only-filesystem error (and/or a direct RO mount check), and the readiness-503/liveliness-200 split
Explains why external monitoring stayed green: liveliness/master-key/caddy probes don't exercise the DB-backed key-auth path
Rejects LiteLLM config/virtual-key misconfiguration as the cause and/or flags postgres corruption risk — recover the FS before restarting the DB

input: Our sec-03 notes claim the Backblaze B2 bucket 'bucket-restic' is ransomware-immutable ('Object Lock GOVERNANCE 30d'). Auditing with the B2 API I see isFileLockEnabled=true on the bucket — but defaultRetention shows mode=null period=null, and every file version I sample (mini/config, mini data packs) has fileRetention mode=null retainUntilTimestamp=null. The bucket also has a lifecycle rule daysFromHidingToDeleting=30, and the restic clients use an append-only application key. Is our restic history actually immutable? What went wrong, what protection do we REALLY have, and how do I confirm?

source.ref: record 22: bucket-restic fileLock enabled, but no default retention and no per-file retention

reference: No — the documented immutability is NOT in effect. Mechanism: B2 Object Lock 'enabled' (isFileLockEnabled=true) only makes retention POSSIBLE; it locks nothing by itself. Files become immutable only via (a) a default bucket retention policy (would stamp each new upload) or (b) per-file retention set at upload. Neither exists here: defaultRetention mode/period are null and every sampled file version carries fileRetention mode=null retainUntilTimestamp=null — so zero files are lock-protected and GOVERNANCE 30d was never actually configured. Real protections that DO exist: (1) the append-only application key used by mini/rig cannot delete (delete attempts return 401 — proven in mini's nightly log), and (2) the lifecycle rule daysFromHidingToDeleting=30 keeps hidden versions 30 days. Residual risk: the master key (deleteFiles capability, and bypassGovernance if retention existed) sits in plaintext in the laptop's vault file — a laptop compromise allows instant hard-delete of all restic history; real GOVERNANCE default retention would have blocked that for 30d. Confirm: b2_list_buckets (fileLock block: defaultRetention nulls despite isFileLockEnabled=true), b2_list_file_versions sampling (all retention nulls), and negative-test a delete with the append-only key expecting 401. Fix (operator): set default bucket retention GOVERNANCE 30d via b2_update_bucket or S3 put-object-lock-configuration — new uploads then get stamped (note: existing versions stay unprotected unless retention is applied to them).

checklist.desc: Core mechanism: Object Lock 'enabled' on the bucket does not lock anything — immutability requires a default bucket retention policy or per-file retention set at upload, and both are absent (nulls), so zero files are protected
Correctly enumerates the actual existing protections: the append-only application key (deletes rejected/401) and the 30-day hiding-to-deleting lifecycle rule

Identifies the residual risk: the master key (delete-capable) in the laptop vault means a laptop compromise can hard-delete the restic history — which real GOVERNANCE retention would have delayed/blocked
Fix: set a default bucket retention (GOVERNANCE 30d) via b2_update_bucket / S3 object-lock configuration (operator action)
Confirmation probes: bucket fileLock/defaultRetention via list-buckets, sampled file-version retention fields, and/or a negative delete test with the append-only key

input: Every night at exactly 00:00 the NAS drops a fresh ~23MB core dump in the /volume1 root, and the journal shows it comes from immich_server's bundled ffmpeg segfaulting — it's happened 5 nights running now, same time each night. Photos still browse fine. Walk me through how you would diagnose what keeps triggering this and how you'd resolve it durably WITHOUT deleting or risking any photo/video asset, plus how you'd verify the fix and monitor for recurrence.

source.ref: fix-60: Immich cluster: nightly ffmpeg segfault on one corrupt .mov

reference: Root cause (fix-60/SM1, 2026-08-03): one corrupt 2021 iPhone HEVC .mov (asset 8a5d0a66, IMG_3674.mov — a Frame-Cropping side-data block crashes the preview '-skip_frame nointra' decode) never got a thumbnail, so Immich's NIGHTLY QUEUE_GENERATE_THUMBNAILS job (force=false, runs at 00:00) re-queued it forever — each attempt segfaults ffmpeg and dumps a core. Diagnosis: correlate the 00:00 timing with Immich's nightly thumbnail job, pull the crashing ffmpeg args/asset from logs/core, confirm ffprobe reads the file fine and a -c copy remux would NOT change the bitstream (so no cheap repair); Synology core_pattern is a pipe so ulimit -c 0 cannot suppress dumps. Fix = QUARANTINE without touching the asset: generate a synthetic placeholder preview.jpeg (1440x1080 mjpeg) + thumbnail.webp (250x188) inside the container via ffmpeg lavfi color (never decodes the corrupt file), INSERT the two asset_file rows so the asset is no longer 'missing preview' and drops out of the regen queue. Deliberately NO move-aside (risks Immich auto-trashing the asset) and no deletion; original .mov untouched, playback intact, grey placeholder thumbnail. Verify: GET /api/assets/{id}/thumbnail returns 200 for both formats, next nights produce zero new core dumps; remove the stale core.gz. Harden: checks nas-immich-corrupt-mov-quarantined (regression) + nas-immich-ffmpeg-nocrash (class) in checks.d/nas-services.yaml. Follow-up: only a re-encode/repair of the source yields a real thumbnail — do not force-regenerate until then.

checklist.desc: Ties the exact-00:00 recurrence to Immich's scheduled nightly thumbnail/preview generation job re-queueing an asset that still lacks a thumbnail (force=false retries forever), i.e., one undecodable video asset is the trigger
Plans to identify the specific asset from the crash context (logs/core/ffmpeg args) and test-decode it (ffprobe/ffmpeg) before acting

Resolution satisfies the 'missing preview' condition with a synthetic/placeholder preview+thumbnail registered to the asset (so it leaves the regen queue) instead of deleting, re-encoding in place, or moving the original
Explicitly avoids moving or deleting the original file (move-aside/delete risks Immich trashing or losing the asset); original stays playable and untouched
Verification includes the API now serving the thumbnail (e.g., GET /api/assets/{id}/thumbnail 200) and subsequent nights producing no new core dumps; stale core dump cleaned up
Notes that suppressing core dumps (ulimit -c 0 etc.) is not a fix and/or won't even work because the NAS core_pattern is a pipe
Adds regression/class verification checks (e.g., quarantine-intact + no-new-ffmpeg-crash) to the monitoring suite
Recognizes this matches prior recorded work (fix-60 / the fix-45 thumbnail-queue regression class) from the repo/tracker

input: A permissions audit on the NAS flagged the mylar3 container: its config.ini sits at 0644 and contains ~23 credential-class keys, and there are several world-writable (0666/0777) files under its cache and .ComicTagger dirs. It's a LinuxServer.io image and the compose already sets the UMASK env var, yet new files keep landing loose. Walk me through how you'd investigate why the perms keep regressing and fix this durably — so neither a container recreate nor the app's own behavior can reopen it — plus verification and monitoring.

source.ref: fix-53: File-permission regressions: mylar3 writes 0644 secret-bearing config + world-writable cache

reference: Root cause (fix-53/SM2+SM3, 2026-08-02): the LSIO mylar3 image IGNORES the UMASK env — its s6 run script execs `s6-setuidgid abc python3 Mylar.py` with no umask call. Structural fix: set umask at PID 1 via compose `entrypoint: ["/bin/sh","-c","umask 077; exec /init"]` so every supervised process inherits it and a fresh recreate creates config.ini 0600. Then chmod the live config.ini to 0600 and PROVE it holds across an in-app rewrite (mylar rewrites via configparser mode-'w' truncate, which preserves the inode mode — mtime advances, mode stays 0600). The world-writable cache files are NOT fixable by umask at all: mylar itself calls os.umask(0) without restoring (PostProcessor.py/filechecker.py) and hard-codes chmod 0777 (cmtagmylar.py/webviewer.py), so after the first grab the process re-litters 0666/0777. Fix for that class = a recurring guard: DSM Task Scheduler job (every 15 min; NEVER raw crontab on DSM — it gets rewritten) runs mylar3-perms-guard.sh re-securing config.ini 0600, owner-only cache/.ComicTagger, stripping world-write under /volume1/docker/mylar3. Codify: compose entrypoint mirrored to configs/nas/mylar3/ (live==repo), guard scripts mirrored to /volume1/scripts/nas/. Monitor: checks nas-mylar3-umask-guard (entrypoint still sets umask 077 — catches a redeploy dropping the fix) + existing nas-secret-file-perms/nas-worldwritable-sweep stay green.

input: soularr on the NAS keeps grinding: its failed_imports.json denylist has grown to 9 entries and some of those albums are demonstrably 100% complete on disk; a couple of foreign-junk-titled albums under one artist get searched and fail every single cycle; and Lidarr's queue shows 2 downloads that completed days ago but sit stuck at import-failed. input: A port sweep of mini just turned up an unexplained `nc -lvnp 9999` listening on 0.0.0.0 — and journal evidence says it's been there for over two weeks, with one ESTABLISHED connection from another LAN host. The same sweep shows ~85 ports fleet-wide bound to 0.0.0.0 on our flat LAN. Walk me through how you'd triage and remove the rogue listener safely, what you'd do (and NOT do) about the broader all-interfaces surface, and how you'd make sure a new rogue listener can never again sit unnoticed for weeks.

source.ref: fix-51: LAN exposure batch: rogue nc listener on mini (17 days), ~85 fleet ports on 0.0.0.0

reference: Ground truth (fix-51, 2026-08-02): the rogue nc was the single pane of a DETACHED tmux session ('rigshell', created during a July audit as a connectivity test) — tmux detach is exactly how a bare nc outlives its SSH session; the ESTABLISHED conn was leftover from a rig<->mini test. Broader surface: MOST 0.0.0.0 binds are by design (Caddy is the auth edge; docker-proxy publishes on 0.0.0.0) — do NOT firewall live services. Instead codify the intended-exposure baseline: per-host commented allowlist files verification/assets/expected-listeners/{mini,rig,nas}.ports (mini 33/rig 22/nas 45, enum-stable) + a lan-exposure runbook documenting the Caddy-as-auth-edge model. Tripwire: checks lan-listeners-drift-{mini,rig,nas} + listener-drift.sh alarm on ANY NEW all-interface listener not in baseline — negative-tested with a throwaway 0.0.0.0:19191 listener (FAILs, clears when gone). Real segmentation is deferred to ha-19 IoT-VLAN work. (Also in batch: BookLogr registration deliberately left open per operator, posture recorded not asserted.)

input: The rig is meant to be a 24/7 host, but it just spent 27 hours down because someone tapped the front power button. While digging I also found: journal timestamps that run ~4 hours off after boots, an avahi hostname-conflict storm that keeps renaming the host on mDNS, one user-level unit with tens of thousands of restarts, and — after the last reboot — the GPU containers (llama-swap/ComfyUI) refused to start until poked manually. Plan a full hardening pass to make this box genuinely 24/7: root causes, fixes, ordering, codification, and the checks you'd add.

source.ref: fix-64: Rig 24/7 host-stability cluster (poweroff, RTC skew, mDNS storm, crash-loops, stale CDI)

reference: Ground truth (fix-64, 2026-08-03): (1) Power key: logind HandlePowerKey=ignore + polkit deny of desktop/loginctl power-off — root CLI poweroff still works (operator protocol documented); runtime-verified. (2) Clock: keep RTC in UTC (timedatectl set-local-rtc 0 — a local-RTC Windows-dual-boot skew was falsifying journals ~4h), enable systemd-time-wait-sync, and order time-sensitive units (immich-ml, playit) After=time-sync.target; controlled reboot confirms no skew. (3) mDNS storm root cause = TWO :5353 responders — systemd-resolved MulticastDNS AND avahi both answering; fix = disable resolved's MulticastDNS + restrict avahi to allow-interfaces=enp10s0 → hostname resolves, 0 conflicts. (4) Crash-loop: the moondeckbuddy user unit disabled+stopped (76k restarts); add crash-recurrence monitoring; key game containers confirmed restart=unless-stopped. (5) GPU-after-reboot: reboot renumbered /dev/dri (card1->card0) leaving a STALE NVIDIA CDI spec that blocked llama-swap/comfyui — fix = nvidia-cdi-refresh.service regenerates the CDI spec before docker starts each boot. Codify all under configs/host/rig/{logind,polkit,resolved,avahi,ufw,nvidia-cdi,immich-ml,playit-udp-guard}/ (rig host config is doc-mirrored, not ansible-managed) + wiki runbook rig-host-stability.md. Six checks: rig-poweroff-inhibit, rig-clock-sane (cross-checked against mini's vantage since the rig's own clock is the suspect), rig-no-crashloop-unit, rig-ml-window-catchup-clean, rig-crash-storm-quiet, rig-mdns-fw-quiet — all run from the mini runner.

checklist.desc: Power-button fix inhibits at the host-policy layer (logind HandlePowerKey=ignore, optionally polkit-denying desktop/session power-off) while preserving an intentional admin/root shutdown path
Clock fix keeps the RTC in UTC (set-local-rtc 0) and gates time-sensitive units on time-sync (systemd-time-wait-sync / After=time-sync.target), verified via a controlled reboot
Diagnoses the avahi conflict storm as two concurrent mDNS responders on :5353 (systemd-resolved MulticastDNS + avahi) and disables/scopes one of them
Explains the GPU-containers-after-reboot failure as stale NVIDIA CDI device specs after /dev/dri renumbering, fixed by regenerating CDI before docker at every boot

input: Bazarr on the NAS hasn't fetched a single subtitle in days — the wanted backlog reads ~2,900 episodes and ~29 movies — yet our Bazarr monitoring check is green. In settings, the enabled-providers list is now EMPTY even though we definitely had a provider configured and working before. Nothing obvious in our configs changed. The NAS is also under heavy I/O load right now. Walk me through diagnosis, how you'd restore subtitle fetching, how you'd prove it's really fixed, and how you'd close the monitoring gap — plus what you would deliberately NOT do right away.

source.ref: fix-59: Bazarr has ZERO subtitle providers enabled — backlog can never fetch while the check stays green

reference: Ground truth (fix-59/SH7, 2026-08-03): the configured provider (Podnapisi) was REMOVED FROM BAZARR ITSELF in the image version the stack had digest-pinned to (v1.6.0-ls356, pinned during fix-38) — on restart Bazarr reconciled the now-unknown provider out of enabled_providers, leaving []. The check stayed green because it probed the producer side (bazarr-synced-from-arrs) — a mandate-1 liveness-vs-consumer gap. Restoring: the operator's preferred replacement (subsource) turned out to REQUIRE an api_key the vault lacks (ConfigurationError on enable) — so verify a provider's auth requirements before relying on it; enabled the genuinely anonymous gestdown (Addic7ed API, TV) + yifysubtitles (movies). Consumer-end proof: an actual English .srt landed beside the video for a real episode (The Musketeers S03E10, gestdown, score ~87%) and Bazarr's download history incremented 0→1. Monitoring fix: new consumer check bazarr-providers-can-fetch asserting enabled>=1 AND >=1 provider in Good status AND episode+movie download history >=1. Deliberately NOT done: mass-searching the ~2,900-item backlog immediately — the NAS was I/O-saturated; drain throttled later. Codified compose comment repo+live, wiki rebuilt. Follow-ups: optional provider account/api_key into the vault for higher coverage; consider score-cutoff tolerance so ~86-score subs auto-download.

input: I've lost trust in parts of our verification suite. Concretely: one version-comparison check has reported the identical value on every run for months regardless of upstream releases; another check started emitting completely empty output around the time its target service added authentication; a third blows through its 60-second budget every single run and shows permanently dark; and separately a NAS 'docker health' self-heal task has been paging every 15 minutes for hours while accomplishing nothing. Walk me through how you'd audit and repair each failure mode, and the design rules you'd apply so the repaired checks report TRUE state within budget without becoming noise.

source.ref: fix-62: Check quality + coverage batch: structurally-broken checks + no-op self-heal page storm

reference: Ground truth (fix-62, 2026-08-03): (1) Constant-value check = parser anchored to the WRONG line — edge-plex-version-current grepped 'version=' and hit the XML declaration ('1.0' forever, comparison could never fire); fix = anchor the parse to the real element (MediaContainer), and ACCEPT that the repaired check may then legitimately FAIL (it correctly reported VERSION_STALE — report true state, don't chase green; the underlying update is a separate deferred task). (2) Empty-output-since-auth = the service (Stash) added auth and anonymous GraphQL now 401s; fix = send the API key from env (vault-backed, added to /etc/verification/env + env.example) and ALWAYS emit the http_code so failure modes are visible; negative-test that no-auth yields 401. (3) Budget-blowing check = an UNBOUNDED ssh find over a huge NAS tree (6m55s vs 60s); fix = achieve the SAME OUTCOME via an indexed/cheap query (Immich search API createdAfter — 0.15s, zero NAS filesystem I/O) rather than raising the timeout. (4) Related de-flap rule: a probe with zero margin between its curl timeout and observed latency gets explicit margin + min_consecutive_fails>=2. (5) Self-heal page storm root causes: the script expected HTTP 200 but the service's HEALTHY response is a 302 login redirect, and its remediation ('compose up --no-recreate') is a NO-OP on an up-but-dead container, with no backoff — so it paged every 15 min forever; fix = accept the service's real healthy codes (200,302), restart-not-up semantics for wedged-but-running containers (rate-limited), and per-service backoff/dedup state (never page on a no-op; page once per incident then back off ~4h; one recovery page), validated with a scenario dry-run harness. All changed checks re-run audit-safely (separate VERIFICATION_STATE_DIR + --no-notify) before deploy; deploy byte-identical to the mini runner.

checklist.desc: Constant-value check: suspects the parser is matching the wrong line/element (e.g., a header or XML declaration instead of the real field), fixes the anchor, and explicitly accepts the repaired check may now legitimately FAIL — the goal is true state, not green

Empty-output check: correlates with the service having added auth, wires the credential from env/vault into the probe, ensures the check always emits the HTTP status so failures are diagnosable, and negative-tests the unauthenticated path
Over-budget check: replaces the unbounded filesystem scan with an equivalent-outcome cheap/indexed query (API or DB) instead of just raising the timeout — avoiding load on the target host

Self-heal storm: identifies BOTH root causes — healthy-status mismatch (service's normal response is a redirect, not 200) AND a no-op remediation with no backoff — and fixes with real healthy-code acceptance, restart-semantics for wedged containers, and per-incident dedup/backoff so no-ops never page
Validates all changed checks in an audit-safe run (isolated state dir, notifications suppressed) before deploying to the live runner
Applies a de-flap rule for tight-latency probes: timeout margin plus minimum-consecutive-fails before alerting

input: I want to extend the mini journaling pipeline with optional voice notes: when a Memos #journal entry carries an audio attachment, the n8n analyze workflow should transcribe it using the local faster-whisper container and feed the transcript into the coach LLM's context. Two hard requirements: text-only memos must be completely unaffected, and whisper being down must NEVER block or degrade the existing text path. Walk me through the wiring plan — detection, fetch, transcription call, merge, failure handling, deployment — and how you'd verify it truly works end to end.

source.ref: journal-04: Wire optional server-side faster-whisper transcription branch into journal-analyze

reference: Ground truth (journal-04, 2026-07-23): detection = the Guard reads memo.attachments[] carried INLINE (snake_case) in the memos.memo.created webhook payload — no extra API call, so the text path pays nothing; an IF node routes only the first audio/* attachment into the branch (text-only memos take IF->false and the branch nodes never execute). Fetch = Memos binary at /file/{attachment}/{filename} with Bearer PAT (Memos 0.29: resources are ATTACHMENTS, POST /api/v1/attachments). Transcribe = faster-whisper at the CONTAINER port :8000 /v1/audio/transcriptions (multipart, Systran/faster-whisper-small CPU). Merge appends a '[Voice note transcript]' section and rebuilds the LLM messages BEFORE the coach call. Fail-safe: BOTH HTTP nodes are continue-on-error and Merge falls back to the Guard's text-only messages — whisper down never blocks the primary path; the Guard also relaxes its empty-body drop when audio is present so a voice-only entry still gets analyzed. Config via non-secret env WHISPER_BASE_URL/WHISPER_MODEL (compose + .env.example; expressions default so unset still works). Deployment trap: n8n 2.x requires import + `publish:workflow` + container restart — flipping active=1 in the DB does NOT arm the webhook; verify exactly one webhook_entity row. E2E proof: post a #journal memo with a spoken .wav and assert the coach reflection references content that appears ONLY in the audio (e.g., unique spoken words), with EXACTLY ONE comment posted (loop guard held despite the comment-created events); separately confirm a text-only memo skips the branch. Monitoring: daily consumer check journaling-whisper-transcribes performs a REAL transcription of a bundled probe WAV — not a /health liveness ping.

checklist.desc: Branch detection reads the audio attachment straight from the webhook payload (attachments carried inline) and text-only memos skip the entire branch via the gate — zero cost/change to the text path
Transcription call targets the faster-whisper OpenAI-style endpoint (/v1/audio/transcriptions, multipart) reached at the whisper CONTAINER's internal port from n8n
Fail-safe design: the branch's HTTP nodes continue on error and the merge falls back to the original text-only LLM messages, so whisper being down can never block or degrade the primary path
Deployment accounts for the n8n 2.x arming trap: the workflow must be published (publish:workflow) and the container restarted — setting the DB active flag alone does not register the webhook

E2E verification proves the audio actually flowed: the generated reflection references content present ONLY in the spoken audio, and the loop guard still yields exactly one comment; a text-only memo is shown to skip the branch
Ongoing monitoring is a consumer check performing a real transcription of a bundled probe audio file, not a /health or model-list liveness ping

input: On the rig, restic-backup.service, ansible-pull.service, and logrotate.service all started failing at the same time, the palworld container flipped unhealthy with its REST port dead, and LiteLLM is returning 503 no_db_connection to every virtual-key client even though /health/liveliness still returns 200 — and docker ps shows everything Up (healthy). What single condition explains all of this, how do I confirm it in one command, why won't a plain reboot fix it, and what's the documented recovery order?
reference: The rig's root btrfs remounted READ-ONLY after metadata corruption (the fix-20 incident class). Cause: the marginal PCIe link on the WD SN570 OS NVMe corrupts a metadata write in flight — a lost/torn write under a valid checksum (btrfs device stats shows 0 errors; btrfs check shows 'parent transid verify failed', e.g. wanted 16495 found 16087). Everything cascades from ro: writers fail (restic/ansible-pull/logrotate), palworld can't write saves, litellm-db Postgres segfaults on WAL write so virtual-key (DB-auth) calls 503 while master-key liveness stays 200, and docker ps LIES (daemon can't persist state) — trust docker inspect. Confirm: ssh rig 'findmnt -no OPTIONS / | cut -d, -f1' -> ro (exactly what the rig-root-fs-writable check probes with a real write). A plain reboot does NOT fix it: btrfs sets the error state, refuses rw remount after error, and re-hits the bad leaf on every mount, so the box boots to emergency mode with / mounted ro. Recovery order (order matters): (1) SALVAGE FIRST while the fs is still readable ro — nothing after the last restic run is backed up; scp/SFTP unavailable, so stream a tar over raw TCP (nc listener on mini, tar|socat on rig) covering saves, AMP data, litellm-db/open-webui docker volumes, /etc; (2) power off and RESEAT the NVMe, ideally a different M.2 slot (heals the cause; repair only fixes the damage); (3) OFFLINE repair from a Linux live USB with btrfs-progs: btrfs check --readonly, then --repair, then --readonly again which MUST be clean — select the device by UUID (e4b84b06-...) because nvmeN renumbers; never loop --repair — if it can't fix, restore from the last pre-corruption restic snapshot; (4) boot rw, restart docker/stacks, verify litellm-db Postgres came up clean (it died mid-write; restore its volume from salvage if not), run restic-backup.service to close the gap, and confirm the fix-20 checks green (rig-root-fs-writable, rig-litellm-vkey-e2e, etc.). If corruption recurs after a reseat, replace the SN570.

checklist.desc: Identifies the single condition: the root filesystem (btrfs) has remounted read-only due to metadata corruption / btrfs error state
Gives the confirm command: findmnt on / showing 'ro' (or an equivalent real write probe), i.e. what rig-root-fs-writable checks
Warns docker ps is untrustworthy during this incident (daemon can't persist state) and says to use docker inspect instead
Explains a plain reboot won't fix it — btrfs refuses rw remount after the error / boots to emergency mode; repair must be OFFLINE from a live USB via btrfs check --repair
Puts salvage FIRST in the recovery order: pull un-backed-up data while the fs is still readable, streamed over raw TCP (nc/socat) since scp/SFTP is unavailable
Names the hardware root cause — marginal PCIe link on the WD SN570 OS NVMe (lost write despite 0 device-stats errors) — and the reseat (different M.2 slot) / replace-if-recurs remedy
Mentions selecting the filesystem by UUID during offline repair because nvme device numbering shifts, or that a clean post-repair --readonly check is required before rebooting

input: Walk me through the house DNS design: which resolvers does DHCP hand out on the client VLANs and in what order, what upstream does each hop use, and — when the mini goes down — why do users report wiki.tabaska.us and every other *.tabaska.us site dead while Google still works and DNS lookups for those names still succeed?
reference: DHCP on every client VLAN hands out three resolvers, fail-open in order: #1 192.168.10.2 mini AdGuard -> local Unbound (recursive, DNSSEC — no upstream sees queries); #2 192.168.10.4 NAS AdGuard -> public DoT (tls://1.1.1.1, tls://9.9.9.9) deliberately independent of the mini; #3 192.168.10.1 UniFi gateway -> bare internet DNS. Both AdGuards carry the split-horizon rewrite *.tabaska.us -> 192.168.10.2. Design intent: mini down => clients fall to the NAS (filtering + local names survive); mini AND NAS down => gateway (internet survives, local names/filtering gone). The 'filtering off must never mean internet off' rule dates from the 2026-07-03 incident where a mini reboot killed DNS house-wide. When the mini is down, *.tabaska.us HTTPS fails NOT because of DNS — the NAS AdGuard still rewrites the names to 192.168.10.2 — but because Caddy (the reverse proxy behind that IP, sole TLS edge) lives on the mini and is down with it. Direct-port services keep working: Immich 192.168.10.4:2283, Plex, DSM, HA :8123. Per-hop testing: dig @each-IP for an external name plus wiki.tabaska.us (expect 192.168.10.2 from both AdGuards); the scripted drill is scripts/network/dns-resilience-verify.sh.

checklist.desc: States the three-resolver DHCP handout in order: 192.168.10.2 (mini AdGuard), 192.168.10.4 (NAS AdGuard), 192.168.10.1 (gateway)
Gives each hop's upstream: mini AdGuard -> local Unbound (recursive/DNSSEC); NAS AdGuard -> public DoT (1.1.1.1 / 9.9.9.9) deliberately independent; gateway -> plain internet DNS
States both AdGuards rewrite *.tabaska.us -> 192.168.10.2 (split-horizon), so local names survive a mini outage
Explains the mini-down symptom correctly: DNS still resolves via the NAS rewrite but Caddy (the proxy/TLS edge at that IP) is down with the mini — it is a proxy outage, not a DNS outage
Notes direct-port access keeps working during a mini outage (e.g. Immich 192.168.10.4:2283, DSM, Plex, HA :8123)
Mentions per-hop dig testing or the scripted drill (scripts/network/dns-resilience-verify.sh)

input: Explain our off-site backup immutability design on Backblaze B2: which bucket is retention-locked and how, why the other backup bucket is handled differently, how restic's forget/prune still work under the lock, and what happened to the B2 master application key.
reference: Target model is 3-2-1-1-0 (one immutable copy). bucket-restic (mini+rig restic repos) has B2 Object Lock with DEFAULT RETENTION GOVERNANCE 30 DAYS (fix-22, 2026-07-17), plus a one-time backfill that locked all 1174 pre-existing pack versions; new uploads are locked automatically at upload, so the hosts' APPEND-ONLY keys need no extra capabilities. restic forget/prune still work because restic >=0.19 deletes by HIDING files, and the B2 lifecycle rule daysFromHidingToDeleting: 30 only hard-deletes after both the hide window and the retention have passed. bucket-hyper-backup (NAS Hyper Backup) is DELIBERATELY NOT locked (accepted finding M37): Hyper Backup's Smart Recycle rotation must delete old versions and retention would break it; compensating controls are that the content is client-side encrypted and the delete-capable master key is out of the vault. The B2 MASTER KEY was retired from the vault because it carries deleteFiles + bypassGovernance (a laptop/vault compromise could hard-delete everything despite GOVERNANCE); day-to-day access is the scoped read-only b2-ops key (vault backblaze_b2.ops_key_id / ops_key, list/read only), and bucket administration uses the offline master key via scripts/backup/b2-apply-bucket-policy.py (idempotent re-apply + backfill). Daily guards include b2-restic-immutable (crit — asserts the retention config AND live-attempts a delete with the vault key expecting HTTP 401), b2-bucket-policy (bucket-set manifest), and restic-snapshot-hygiene checks.

checklist.desc: States bucket-restic has B2 Object Lock default retention GOVERNANCE 30 days

Explains bucket-hyper-backup is deliberately NOT locked because Hyper Backup's Smart Recycle rotation must delete old versions, with compensating controls (client-side encryption and/or master key kept offline)
Explains restic prune compatibility: restic (>=0.19) deletes by hiding and the lifecycle rule (daysFromHidingToDeleting 30) hard-deletes only after hide window + retention pass

States the master key was retired from the vault (it carries deleteFiles/bypassGovernance); day-to-day uses a scoped read-only ops key and bucket admin uses the offline master key via the policy script
Notes mini/rig push with append-only keys and locking happens automatically at upload (no extra key capabilities needed)
Mentions the live negative test (b2-restic-immutable attempts a delete expecting 401) or frames the design as the 3-2-1-1-0 target's immutable leg

input: I need to restore the Immich Postgres database on the NAS from the nightly dump — photos are on disk but albums, faces, and metadata are wrong after an incident. What's the documented restore procedure, start to finish?
reference: Immich data = photo files under UPLOAD_LOCATION plus the Postgres DB; files without the DB lose albums/faces/metadata. Procedure (on the NAS, in /volume1/docker/immich): (1) stop the app but keep the DB up: sudo docker compose stop immich-server immich-machine-learning; (2) pick the newest .sql.gz from /volume1/docker/immich/backups/ (produced by the nightly NAS Task Scheduler dump, dead-manned as immich-dump-nas); (3) restore into the running postgres container: gunzip -c backups/<dump>.sql.gz | sudo docker exec -i immich_postgres psql -U <DB_USERNAME> -d <DB_DATABASE_NAME> — for a clean restore, drop and recreate the database first via psql in the same container; (4) sudo docker compose up -d, then verify curl http://192.168.10.4:2283/api/server/ping returns {"res":"pong"} and spot-check by logging in to confirm albums and people are intact. Credentials come from /volume1/docker/immich/.env, never from a doc.

checklist.desc: Stops the app containers (immich-server + immich-machine-learning) while keeping the postgres container running
Locates the dumps at /volume1/docker/immich/backups/ (newest .sql.gz; nightly scheduled dump)
Restores by piping the gunzip'd dump into psql inside the immich_postgres container (docker exec -i ... psql -U ... -d ...)
Recommends dropping/recreating the database first for a clean restore
Verifies with compose up -d plus the /api/server/ping pong probe and an album/people spot-check; DB credentials read from the stack's .env

input: I added a new vhost to the Caddyfile on the mini (and mirrored it into the repo), but browsers get a TLS 'internal error' for the new name while every other *.tabaska.us site works fine. The backend itself is up. What's the documented failure mode here, the exact fix, and the verification check that exists for precisely this?
reference: Failure mode: the Caddyfile was edited but caddy was never RELOADED — the RUNNING config, not the file on disk, serves traffic, so the running instance has no route or cert for the new vhost and clients get a TLS internal error (exactly the llamaswap incident, which ran 3 days). Fix: validate then graceful zero-downtime reload inside the container: ssh mini 'docker exec caddy caddy validate --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile && docker exec caddy caddy reload --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile', then confirm the consumer path: curl -sk --resolve <name>.tabaska.us:443:192.168.10.2 https://<name>.tabaska.us/. The check is mini-caddy-live-config-current (added by fix-32): it adapts the on-disk Caddyfile and diffs its vhost set against the admin-API running config, reporting missing_live (on disk but not served — this case) and extra_live (removed from disk but still served). Standing rule: every Caddyfile edit must end with a reload — edit-without-reload is an incomplete change — and the edit must be mirrored to the repo Caddyfile plus the /opt/stacks git repo. Related context: the LAN wildcard *.tabaska.us -> 192.168.10.2 makes ANY unknown name resolve to caddy and fail the TLS handshake, which is normal for retired names, not an incident.

checklist.desc: Diagnoses edit-without-reload: the running caddy config serves traffic, not the on-disk Caddyfile, so the new vhost has no route/cert until a reload
Gives the fix: caddy validate followed by caddy reload (docker exec into the caddy container; graceful/zero-downtime)
Names mini-caddy-live-config-current (or accurately describes the disk-vs-admin-API vhost diff with missing_live/extra_live outputs)
Verifies the consumer end with curl --resolve <name>.tabaska.us:443:192.168.10.2 (or equivalent through-the-proxy probe)
States the standing rule that every Caddyfile edit ends with a reload (and mirrors to repo/anti-drift), or notes the wildcard makes unknown names fail TLS normally

input: What's our documented container image update policy and end-to-end flow — from learning an update exists to it running on a host? Include how Immich and Caddy differ from the standard path, and how we'd roll back.
reference: Policy: NO blind auto-updates, ever — every image pinned to an exact tag; watchtower-style always-pull-latest is banned. Flow: Diun on the mini watches every running container's image and posts to ntfy topic 'diun' when a new tag appears (awareness only, no action) -> operator reads release notes (esp. breaking-change projects: Immich majors, Postgres majors, Caddy, the *arrs) -> bump the pin in the REPO compose first (configs/docker-stack/stacks/<name>/compose.yaml or configs/nas/<name>/ — repo is the source of truth, never bump only on the host) -> commit to home-config, run scripts/docs/publish-deploy.sh, mirror into /opt/stacks/<name>/compose.yaml and commit that repo too -> apply: on mini 'docker compose pull && docker compose up -d'; NAS stacks via Container Manager -> project -> Action -> Clean & rebuild -> verify (compose ps, logs tail, curl the https vhost) -> regenerate wiki service pages (gen-wiki-services.py + build-wiki.sh) since the pin is on the page. Rollback: the previous pin is one git revert away + compose up -d — but DB-migrating apps like Immich may not roll back cleanly, which is why release notes come first. Special cases: Immich is pinned via IMMICH_VERSION in .env on the NAS with DB/Redis images digest-pinned to match the release (bump together); Caddy is a custom-built image (Cloudflare DNS module) — bump the base in stacks/caddy/Dockerfile and docker compose build. Meta-check: docker inspect --format {{.Config.Image}} must match the compose pin in git.

checklist.desc: States the policy: exact-tag pins everywhere, no auto-updaters (watchtower-style banned)
Describes Diun -> ntfy topic 'diun' as awareness-only, followed by reading release notes and bumping the pin in the REPO first (repo = source of truth)
Gives the apply path: commit+publish then mirror to /opt/stacks; mini = compose pull + up -d; NAS = Container Manager Clean & rebuild; then verify service + logs
Immich special case: pinned via IMMICH_VERSION in .env on the NAS; DB/Redis digest-pinned and bumped together with the release
Caddy special case: custom-built image with the Cloudflare DNS module — bump the Dockerfile base and rebuild
Rollback = git revert the pin + compose up -d, with the caveat that DB-migrating apps may not roll back cleanly

input: Does the fleet actually have UPS protection right now? I found NUT/upsmon config lying around on the mini — what's the story behind it, what damage did it once cause, and what exactly would I do if I bought a UPS for the NAS tomorrow?
reference: No — no UPS is attached to the fleet and UPS-triggered clean shutdown is NOT in place; this is an accepted state folded into deferred tracker item glue-01 (no UPS budget). History: the mini was configured as a NUT netclient (upsmon) monitoring a UPS supposedly on the NAS over TCP 3493, but the NAS end never existed — no UPS hardware and DSM UPS support disabled, so upsd never listened. upsmon retried every ~5 s for 7+ days (~120k 'Connection refused' errors), filling the persistent journal to 4.1 GB while providing zero protection (liveness looked fine; the consumer end never existed). fix-31 remediation: (1) retired nut-monitor via nut-client-retire.sh — stop + disable + MASK the unit (masked = cannot be started by dependency or accident), MODE=none in /etc/nut/nut.conf, MONITOR block commented; (2) guarded the setup script nut-client-ubuntu.sh to refuse to run unless NUT_REENABLE=1 is set; (3) capped journald on mini+rig (SystemMaxUse=1G, SystemMaxFileSize=128M via configs/host/common/journald/10-size-cap.conf + vacuum; mini went 4.1G -> 1.0G; NAS excluded — DSM rotates its own logs). Guards: nut-monitor-retired (masked+inactive AND no recent connect-failed spam), journal-not-bloated-mini/rig (<2G). Re-enable when a UPS is bought: on the NAS enable DSM UPS support + 'Enable network UPS server' + add mini's IP 192.168.10.2 to Permitted DiskStation Devices, confirm upsd listening on 3493; on mini run sudo NUT_REENABLE=1 NAS_IP=192.168.10.4 .../nut-client-ubuntu.sh; verify end-to-end with upsc ups@192.168.10.4 and replace the retired-check with a consumer check.

checklist.desc: Answers no: no UPS attached, clean-shutdown not in place, deliberately accepted/deferred (glue-01) and the NUT client was retired
Explains the past damage mechanism: upsmon retrying an unreachable/never-existing NAS UPS server (port 3493) every few seconds filled the journal to ~4 GB while providing zero protection
States the retirement was stop+disable+MASK (masked so nothing can restart it) plus MODE=none, and the setup script is gated behind NUT_REENABLE=1
Mentions the journald size cap now on mini+rig (SystemMaxUse=1G / 128M files) and/or the journal-not-bloated (<2G) checks
Gives the re-enable path: DSM UPS support + network UPS server + permit mini's IP, confirm 3493 listening, then the guarded script with NUT_REENABLE=1, verified with upsc

input: From the public internet, what is supposed to be reachable on our home WAN IP, and what should exist in public DNS for tabaska.us? And how would we actually notice if something extra got opened or published?
reference: Intended posture: EXACTLY ONE inbound WAN port open — 32400 -> NAS Plex (Plex Remote Access, intentional operator decision so household users can stream without Tailscale). It is a MANUAL port-forward on the operator-managed UniFi Dream Wall; the gateway offers NO UPnP IGD and NO NAT-PMP (verified with upnpc/natpmpc), so no LAN device can silently open additional ports — a new open port means someone added a manual forward (or verification is broken). Plex's unauthenticated /identity endpoint is internet-reachable by design (version + machineIdentifier disclosure); everything token-gated stays token-gated. Public DNS: the tabaska.us Cloudflare zone contains ZERO host records — only Proton mail records, playit.gg NS delegations (minecraft/palworld/bedrock), and TXT; every service name is NXDOMAIN publicly and resolves only via the AdGuard split-horizon rewrites (the old www -> 192.168.10.2 RFC1918-leaking A record was deleted 2026-07-17). Detection: verification/checks.d/edge.yaml — a WAN port sweep run FROM THE SEEDBOX (a true off-net vantage; LAN-side probes only test NAT hairpin) that pages crit on any port besides 32400; a pinned machineIdentifier probe of the exposed Plex (something else answering = incident, close the forward first); a CVE-posture warn if the exposed Plex build lags the latest Synology release >14 days; and a Cloudflare zone audit failing on any private-IP record.

checklist.desc: States exactly one WAN port is open: 32400 forwarded to NAS Plex, an intentional manual forward for household remote streaming
States the gateway offers no UPnP/NAT-PMP, so any new open port implies a manual (human/GUI) change
States public tabaska.us DNS has no host/service records — only mail records, playit NS delegations, and TXT; service names are NXDOMAIN publicly and exist only via AdGuard split-horizon rewrites
Detection includes a WAN port sweep run from the seedbox as an off-net vantage, noting LAN-side probes only test NAT hairpin
Mentions at least one further guard: pinned Plex machineIdentifier probe, Plex version-staleness (>14d) warn, or the Cloudflare zone private-IP audit

input: Nearly all of our alerting lives on the mini — ntfy, Healthchecks, Uptime Kuma, the verification tiers. So if the mini dies outright, what documented mechanism still pages me, how exactly does it work (where it runs, what it probes, thresholds, delivery path), and why was its delivery path judged acceptable in a deliberately no-cloud fleet?
reference: The off-mini dead-man (fix-63, closing fleet-sweep SH19: nothing on mini can report mini dead). It runs on the RIG (24/7): mini-deadman.timer -> /usr/local/bin/mini-deadman.sh (canonical source configs/host/rig/mini-deadman/). Every 5 minutes it TCP-probes mini's Caddy TLS edge at 192.168.10.2:443; THREE consecutive misses (~15 min, tolerating a Caddy restart) trigger a MAX-PRIORITY page published DIRECTLY to the PUBLIC ntfy.sh server on a secret topic (vault alerting.mini_deadman_ntfy_topic), bypassing mini entirely; DNS is made mini-independent by resolving ntfy.sh against a public resolver (mini hosts primary DNS). It re-pages hourly while down and sends a RECOVERED notice when the edge returns. Why the public relay is acceptable despite the no-cloud stance (foss-03): a dead-man is only meaningful OUTSIDE the thing it watches; iOS push for the self-hosted ntfy already relays through ntfy.sh anyway; and the payload is a bare alert with no secrets — the topic name itself is the read secret. It was chosen over an external hosted heartbeat because a robust self-hosted off-mini watcher (the rig) already exists and needs no external account. Residual gap: if the rig is ALSO down (whole-house power loss) there is no page — accepted as self-evident, phone on cellular. Operator requirement: subscribe the phone's ntfy app to the ntfy.sh SERVER (not the self-hosted one) on that topic with a loud sound. Self-test: MINI_DEADMAN_FORCE_DOWN=1 FAIL_THRESHOLD=1 run, read the message back off ntfy.sh; armed-ness is guarded by the alert-offmini-deadman-armed check.

checklist.desc: Places the watcher on the rig as a systemd timer running every 5 minutes, probing mini's Caddy TLS edge (192.168.10.2:443 TCP)
States the trip threshold: ~3 consecutive misses (~15 min, tolerates a Caddy restart), with hourly re-pages while down and a recovery notice
States delivery goes directly to the PUBLIC ntfy.sh server on a secret topic (vault alerting.mini_deadman_ntfy_topic), bypassing mini entirely
Notes DNS for the page path is mini-independent (public resolver) because mini hosts primary DNS
Gives the no-cloud rationale: a dead-man must live outside what it watches; iOS ntfy push already relays via ntfy.sh; payload carries no secrets (the topic name is the read secret)
Acknowledges the residual gap (rig also down = no page, accepted) and/or that the phone must subscribe to the topic on ntfy.sh itself for it to be received
